newsitem.title: INDIA: Intel says India must boost computer investment.
newsitem.headline: Intel says India must boost computer investment.

text.p: India, striving to become a world leader in information technology, must boost investment and education in computers in order to achieve its goal, the president of Intel Corp said on Friday.

"It really requires the government to be involved and facilitate infrastructure," said Craig Barrett, who is designated to take over as the next chief executive officer of the world's largest computer chip maker.

Barrett, on a two-day visit to India to boost the use of computers, told a news conference that Intel planned to invest tens of millions of dollars to promote computers in the nation. He also addressed a seminar on the future of the industry.

The visit of Intel's CEO-designate came three months after a much-publicised visit by Bill Gates, the chairman of Microsoft Corp, the world's biggest software company. The tours are seen as an indication of India's growth potential linked to its huge community of software experts.

Barrett said Intel had expanded from sales and marketing development to software engineering in other Asian countries and hinted that it could do the same in India. "I don't guarantee that it will follow, but it is a road map," he said.
Intel officials said the Indian government had approved an investment of more than $100 million for Intel to set up a wholly owned subsidiary in India.
Barrett said India's business community, academic institutions and authorities promoting technical education must pool their efforts to promote the use of computers.
The technology gap between developed countries and India was closing swiftly as newer chip technologies have enabled latecomers like India to leapfrog, he said.

India's personal computer sales were growing at an attractive rate of more than 50 percent, but investment in information technology was less than 0.5 percent of gross domestic product, sharply lower than three to four percent in some other Asian countries, Barrett said.
"This expenditure will have to increase," Barrett said, noting that the penetration level of computers and telecommunications in India was well below that in Malaysia and Thailand.
India's personal computer sales in 1996/97 (April-March) rose to around 550,000 units from 362,000 in 1995/96, a spokesman for the Manufacturers Association of Information Technology (MAIT) said.
"This year's (1997/98) forecast is one million PCs. My gut feel is that it would be at least around 800,000," spokesman Vinnie Mehta told Reuters.
India had an estimated 500,000 schools but less than 5,000 had access to computers and only in the bigger cities, Barrett said.
On Friday, Barrett inaugurated a "Cyberskool" to promote multimedia computers made with Intel's chip technology.

India's HCL Hewlett-Packard Ltd, in which U.S. computer maker Hewlett-Packard Co is a joint venture partner, announced an alliance with Intel to develop business desktop personal computers for the Indian market.
